articles.title: Actor Noel Clarke charged with sexual offences
articles.summary: He has been charged with sexual offences including sexual assault, voyeurism and exposure.
articles.body:
Actor Noel Clarke has been charged with sexual offences including sexual assault, voyeurism and exposure.

The Crown Prosecution Service authorised the Metropolitan Police to charge the Doctor Who and Kidulthood star on Wednesday, after a file of evidence was submitted by detectives.

Clarke, 50, from Kensington, west London, was charged with two counts of sexual assault, three charges of voyeurism and one charge of exposure. The offences are alleged to have taken place between 2007 and 2016 and relate to five women.

BBC News has asked his representatives for a comment.

The charges follow an investigation by detectives which began a year ago.

A man, then in his 40s, was first arrested in connection with the investigation on 25 September 2025.

A file of evidence was later given to the CPS who authorised charges.

Clarke will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 21 October at 10:00 BST.

Det Supt Mike Cagney, whose team is leading the investigation, said: "The women connected to these charges continue to receive support from specially trained officers.

"We urge anyone who has been a victim of sexual assault to contact police. The information you provide will be dealt with in the utmost sensitivity and we have trained investigators on hand to support you."

Clarke found fame playing Mickey Smith in Doctor Who between 2005 and 2010, and went on to become a successful actor, writer, producer and director.

articles.title: 'Mum and Dad are still missing after the flooding in the Himalayas'
articles.summary: Prajval Haldia's parents have been missing since since the floods in Tibet and Nepal of 26 August.
articles.body:
Prajval Haldia has has not heard from his parents, Pavan and Kavita, since the devastating floods in the Himalayas two weeks ago.

The last he heard they were enjoying their trip to the mountain range, and were last known to be at Gyirong Port, on the Tibet-Nepal border, on the way to Mount Kailash with a tour group.

Since the devastating floods surged through the area on 26 August, messages from both have stopped, and Prajval has not heard anything of their whereabouts since.

"I think it gets harder to stay positive day by day but we're just trying to keep hope. Maybe no news is good news," said Prajval, who is from Petts Wood in south-east London.

More than 1,300 people were killed in the floods triggered by a glacial collapse near the Nepal-Tibet border, with 5,000 still missing including more than 30 British nationals.

Prajval has been in close contact with the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office but as yet, there is no information on his parents.

"I think the first instinct was obviously for me to go out there and try and do what I can," Prajval explained.

"But, talking to people, talking to the Foreign Office and everyone, I think it's me as someone with no rescue experience or anything like that, I think I'll just create more of a hassle by going out there.

"I think there's very experienced people there, doing very important work. I think it's important to have faith in them to do that job," he added.

Prajval said his parents' pilgrimage had been in the planning "for a while".

"My mum has really wanted to visit this part of the world for a long time, ever since she's seen pictures of it in school textbooks."

He explained that for his parents, "the natural beauty of being in the mountains was also very important".

Prajval said his cousins living nearby have been a "massive support", adding that some more family from India were on the way.

He said he was also receiving support from neighbours and people in the Hindu community.

The local temple, the Sanatan Mandir temple in Coulsdon, has been a place of comfort in recent days.

Sixteen people from the congregation were on a separate pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, and are also missing.

Each evening, prayer services are being held for those missing and for the families affected.

Hearing the songs being played, Prajval said it reminded him of his mum.

"It's a sense of comfort, like it's a similar thing that I'm used to hearing at home," he said.

Sachin Bagla, the manager of the temple, said the mood there was "very sad".

"People are constantly praying and hoping," he explained.

"We know that with every passing day, every passing hour, it becomes more and more difficult. But people are staying together, keeping the faith, and praying to God, offering support in whatever ways they can, especially to the family members."

Bagla explained that the community was also trying to find any practical way to offer support, with fundraisers being launched and volunteers travelling out to the region to help.

Sachin explained that the affected families were being given support by the Foreign Office, and said at the temple "we just pray [for good news] until we are told otherwise".

He added: "We want to stay positive, we want to stay faithful. Keeping our faith in God is very, very important for this community of British Hindus that we are."

He said of those missing in the Himalayas: "We just pray for the people and for God to look after them, wherever they are."

articles.title: Hopes for 'awesome' Channel Islands Pride despite ferry problems
articles.summary: The cancelled ferries have scuppered day trippers but weekend visitors will still be able to attend.
articles.body:
Channel Islands Pride organisers have insisted this year's event will be "awesome" despite the setback of a cancelled inter-island ferry service.

Islands Unlimited, which runs a daily inter-island foot passenger service, has ended the season early due to an engine failure on its MV San Pawl vessel.

Channel Islands Pride is due to take place from Friday to Sunday with the main village area at La Vallette Bathing Pools in St Peter Port, Guernsey.

Ellie Jones, Pride director and chief executive of LGBTQ+ charity Liberate, said the "disappointing" situation would impact about 100 day trippers that she knew of - but added Islands Unlimited "couldn't have done anything more".

The daily ferry service between Guernsey and Jersey, with weekend sailings to Alderney, was due to run until 18 October.

Islands Unlimited said the cause of the problem was found after an extensive technical investigation and it recognised "the disruption and disappointment this will cause, particularly for passengers with upcoming travel plans".

The operator said it fully intended to return in 2027 and would complete the necessary engine replacement and associated works over the coming months and "build greater resilience" into its operation.

"We want to celebrate across the islands and it's going to stop a few people coming," Jones said.

"It was the first time we'd been able to have a day trip for Pride between the islands.

"It's disappointing that hasn't happened but Islands Unlimited couldn't have done anything more and they informed us quickly."

Jones said previously organisers feared the ferry issue would also scupper the scheduled attendance at Pride of choir Lavender Menace .

However, she said another charity had helped them charter a boat for the group and it was hoped most visitors would be heading over for the full weekend via other modes of transport.

Jones said excitement was building for Pride, in part due to the event's new location at the Bathing Pools, while she expected the parade to be "awesome".

"We think it's going to be one of the prettiest Prides in the world," she added.

"The backdrop is absolutely beautiful - the historic seafront at St Peter Port - it's really exciting to see how that all pans out."

articles.title: Cubans are pushed to the breaking point as crises take their toll
articles.summary: Many don’t see relief in sight amid increased U.S. sanctions and longtime economic and financial troubles.
articles.body: HAVANA — Sweltering nights. Water and power shortages. Dwindling fuel and crumbling homes. Limited public transportation and weak cellphone signals. The psychological toll of daily life in Cuba is pushing many to their breaking point on this island of nearly 10 million people, with no relief in sight as a U.S. energy embargo persists and longtime economic and financial troubles deepen. “Before there was hope,” Dr. Yomeidis Felicó Riverón said. “Right now, what people have lost is exactly that.” Felicó Riverón is a primary care physician, but she has embraced an additional role as Cubans grind through their days. “They come and cry about their troubles, because they have no one else to vent to,” she said of her patients. “We end up having to play psychologist.” Parents shield children from Cuba’s realities On a recent sunny afternoon, six girls and one boy crowded around a table as their parents sat in the background, trying to fan away the stifling heat. The children were learning how to make gift bags and perfume, a free workshop that offered them a brief respite from Cuba’s realities. “My son doesn’t know if there’s food or if there’s no food,” Felicó Riverón said, confiding that she never tells him when she doesn’t have money to buy something he wants. Instead, she distracts him: “Let’s go play, let’s go to the park. We’ll come back another day.” Dianne Tamayo was among the mothers present that day. The workshop served as an oasis for her and her daughter. Tamayo socialized and temporarily forgot what awaited at home. “My husband is my rock,” she said. “When I’m going crazy, my husband tells me, ‘Sit down, breathe … let’s put on some music.’” He sometimes has to remind Tamayo that their daughter is coming home from school soon, and that they need to keep their troubles, anxieties and frustrations to themselves. “I do the best I can with the tools I have, but there’s still a moment where I get overwhelmed,” she said. Tears fell as she confided that she doesn’t have anything in her life that relaxes her, and that she has never questioned how to release her feelings about life in Cuba. “They are exterminating us,” she said, “and we remain complacent.” U.S. Embassy issues health alerts Cuba’s crises worsened after U.S. President Donald Trump announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to the Caribbean country. Longtime U.S. sanctions also have taken their toll, Cuba’s government said. From March 2025 to the end of February, “the U.S. policy of economic strangulation” amounted to more than $8 billion, “a record figure,” according to Cuban Foreign Affairs Minister Bruno Rodríguez. Island-wide blackouts have increased this year, and daily outages now surpass 24 hours. As a result, water is often scarce, and small protests have erupted, despite the fear of being detained, as anger and frustration boil over. The situation has worsened to a point that the U.S. Embassy recently issued two public health alerts. On Aug. 28, the embassy noted that “Cuba’s water supply infrastructure is increasingly unstable ” and that there are “residential neighborhoods experiencing long periods without water from municipal or public sources.” On Friday, the embassy warned of an increase in gastrointestinal illnesses linked to the “degradation of the water and energy infrastructure. …. Recent cases have included E. coli, norovirus, Shigella, and other gastrointestinal pathogens.” Water and power shortages persist, but 81-year-old Havana resident Oscar Joaquín López said that he doesn’t dwell on what he lacks. “Why?” López said. “Because it drives you crazy, and nobody is going to drive me crazy.” On a recent afternoon, he leaned against the doorframe of his home as he watched his 58-year-old roommate fill up nearly a dozen plastic containers with water that flowed from a pipe on the street. They had been without water for several days, so they acted quickly. With temperatures hovering above 90 F (32 C), López said that he sits in his doorframe until midnight to catch a breeze from the nearby ocean, a steel pipe nearby to ward off any intruders. After midnight, he goes to bed, hoping the wooden slat he wedged into his window will catch any wind, however slight. Nearby, 62-year-old mason José Laó Faviel dug through overflowing garbage on the street, looking for food to feed his pig and her 10 piglets, because he had none to give them. “What are you going to do?” he said. “We’re living through difficult times.” Minutes later, another man rifled through the same pile of garbage. After opening several bags, he found something to eat. Cubans find solace in family Sweat gathered around Armando Lafita’s brow as the 60-year-old pushed a cart through the crumbling buildings in Old Havana. Authorities have evacuated some residents in the area for safety reasons, but those with nowhere else to live now sleep on the street, ducking inside their building when they need something. Lafita’s cart was filled with red roses and white ginger lilies, Cuba’s national flower. He sells them for 10 to 40 cents a bunch, but sometimes he goes home without a single sale. “Everybody is fighting to survive here,” he said. “It’s getting harder every day.” Like many Cubans, Lafita said the only thing that keeps him going is family: his 19-year-old son. It’s the same reason that 70-year-old José Manuel Borroto Díaz and his 93-year-old mother, Teresita del Rosario González Ricardo, keep going: they have each other. “Our situation is like something out of a movie, but we’re going to press on,” said Borroto, a retired aviation official who was in Angola during Cuba’s military intervention in the 1970s. Across the island, Cubans are pressing on even as the crises deepen, including 90-year-old Lázaro Alfonso Oviedo. He recently attended a weekly gathering to help raise the spirits of elderly people. Oviedo danced and sang in a deep, robust voice “to forget for a little while the suffering the empire puts us through,” he said, referring to the United States.
